title: The clock is a budget
outcomes: Reads a time control such as 10+5 and works out total time and average time per move
Plans a reserve and a per-move average
Tells forced, equal-choice and tempting-move positions apart
Writes a time plan before a game and compares it afterwards

steps.text:
A time control such as **10+5** gives each player 10 minutes at the start and adds 5 seconds after every move that player makes (the *increment*). If your clock reaches zero you usually lose the game on time.
Time is a budget: **average time per move = time you have ÷ moves still to play.**

steps.prompt: Work these out before you read on. Time control 10+5, and you play 40 moves. How many seconds do you have in total, and how many seconds per move on average?

steps.text:
**Answers:** 10 minutes is 600 seconds. Increment: 40 × 5 = 200 seconds. Total 800 seconds, which is 20 seconds per move.
An average hides the point: **spend by position type.** Next you judge three kinds: one legal move, many moves about equal, and a position where a tempting move loses a lot.

steps.title: Where should the time go?
steps.prompt: Each position comes with 2:40 on the clock. Say what kind of position it is, then check. Think about how much clock each deserves.

steps.text: **A budget with a reserve.** Keep some time for the end. Example: 5+0, reserve 60 seconds, 35 moves to play: (300 − 60) ÷ 35 is about 6.9 seconds per move. Forced moves can cost a second or two and bank time for the hard ones. These numbers are a first guess to test in your own games, not a law.

steps.prompt: Two more sums. (1) Control 5+0, reserve 60 seconds, 35 moves: average seconds per move, to one decimal? (2) Control 3+2: how many seconds of increment have you gained after 30 moves?

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** Right now the app gives you the average and names the position types. From the next item on it gives nothing: you decide how much clock the position deserves. A time-per-move record and a post-game summary are planned; if they are built they will be shown to you and not scored.

steps.prompt: Write a time plan for your next game before you start. After the game, compare the plan with what really happened; the gap is the information.

fields.label: Average seconds per move that leaves:
After the game: where did my time actually go?
